setup: A USD 50m bond book holds USD 30m of AA paper (1-year PD 1%, recovery 80%) and USD 20m of BB paper (1-year PD 2.5%, recovery 60%). You are building the 1-year expected credit loss bucket by bucket.
ask: Which bucket contributes more to the expected loss?

options.label: BB, roughly three times as much as AA
AA, because it is the larger holding
options.why: Looked at exposure alone. BB has 2.5 times the default probability and twice the loss rate (40% against 20%), which more than offsets its smaller size.

options.label: About the same
options.why: Assumed the smaller BB position offsets its higher PD. Done properly it is USD 60,000 for AA against USD 200,000 for BB.

takeaway: Expected loss is exposure x PD x loss rate. A riskier name can dominate the total even when it is the smaller position.

setup: One-year bond portfolio: USD 7m of Taylor (PD 6%, recovery 80%) and USD 9m of Simon (PD 5%, recovery 90%).
ask: Portfolio expected loss from default is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 45,000
options.why: Counted only Simon (9m x 5% x 10% = 45,000) and left out the Taylor leg.

options.label: ≈ USD 870,000
options.why: Used exposure x PD and never applied the loss rate (1 - recovery): 420,000 + 450,000.

options.label: ≈ USD 2,300,000
options.why: Used exposure x loss rate and never applied the default probability: 1.4m + 0.9m.

takeaway: EL needs all three ingredients (exposure, PD, 1 - recovery) and is additive across positions.

setup: Two one-year bonds. Bond 1: USD 500,000, PD 5%, recovery 50%. Bond 2: USD 300,000, PD 3%, recovery 30%. The two default together with probability 2%, and their default correlation is 25%.
ask: How does the portfolio expected loss compare with the sum of the two stand-alone expected losses?

options.label: Higher than the sum, because the defaults are positively correlated
options.why: Mixed up expected loss with unexpected loss. Correlation fattens the tail of the loss distribution; it does not move the mean.

options.label: Lower than the sum, because joint defaults overlap
options.why: Treated the 2% joint default as double counting. Expectations add whatever the dependence, so nothing is netted off.

takeaway: Expectation is linear: portfolio EL is the sum of the parts. Correlation matters for unexpected loss, not EL.

setup: A firm's only debt is a 5-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 100m, trading at USD 88m. The risk-free rate is 1%, continuously compounded. You are partway through finding the credit spread.
ask: The bond's continuously compounded yield, before the risk-free rate is taken off, is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 12.8% a year
options.why: Used $-\ln(0.88)$ as it stands and forgot to divide by the 5 years, so the figure is a total over five years, not a yearly rate.

options.label: ≈ 1.6% a year
options.why: That is the spread, not the yield. The risk-free 1% has already been subtracted, which is the last step.

takeaway: A zero-coupon yield is $-\ln(P/F)/T$. Divide by T first, then subtract the risk-free rate.

setup: A firm's only debt is a 6-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 200m, now worth USD 110m. The risk-free rate is 5%, continuously compounded.
ask: The credit spread on the bond (continuous compounding) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 1.7% a year
options.why: Divided by the 6 years twice: the 9.96% yield became 1.66%, and the risk-free rate was then ignored.

options.label: ≈ 13.6% a year
options.why: Used simple growth, (200/110 - 1)/6, as the yield and never subtracted the 5% risk-free rate.

options.label: ≈ 54.8% a year
options.why: Skipped the division by 6 years: $\ln(200/110) - 5\% = 54.8\%$.

takeaway: Spread = $-\ln(P/F)/T - r_f$. Both the 1/T and the subtraction are needed; a spread of tens of percent is a missing 1/T.

setup: Debt with 5 years to maturity has face value USD 1,000 and trades at USD 834. The risk-free rate is 2%, continuously compounded.
ask: The credit spread on this debt is:

options.label: Zero
options.why: Spread is zero only if the price equals the riskless value, $1000e^{-0.02 \times 5} = 904.84$. The market price is well below that.

options.label: Negative
options.why: Read the price discount to face (834 against 1,000) as a sign of a low yield. A lower price than the riskless value means a higher yield, so a positive spread.

takeaway: Price below the riskless value of the same cash flow means yield above the risk-free rate, so the spread is positive.

setup: A 5-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 100m was issued two years ago and now trades at USD 80m. Its credit spread is 2%, continuously compounded. You want the risk-free rate implied by these data.
ask: Which maturity goes into $y = -\ln(P/F)/T$?

options.label: 5 years, the original maturity
options.why: Used the original term. The price is today's, so T is what remains to maturity. This gives y = 4.46% and a risk-free rate of 2.46%.

options.label: 2 years, the time elapsed since issue
options.why: Used the age of the bond. Age plays no part in discounting the remaining payment.

takeaway: Discount over the time remaining, not the original term. The yield is 7.44% and the risk-free rate 5.44%.

setup: A firm's only debt is a 1-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 800m. A Merton-type model gives an expected loss of USD 8.4m and a 0.1% quantile of the bond's future value of USD 503m. Credit VaR is defined as the 99.9th percentile loss in excess of the expected loss.
ask: Compared with the 99.9th percentile loss of USD 297m (800 - 503), the credit VaR is:

options.label: Smaller, by the USD 8.4m expected loss
Equal, since both measure the worst case
options.why: Ignored the "in excess of the expected loss" part of the definition. Credit VaR here is a deviation from the mean, not the raw tail loss.

options.label: Larger, by the USD 8.4m expected loss
options.why: Added EL instead of subtracting it: 297 + 8.4 = 305.4.

takeaway: When credit VaR is defined as the tail loss in excess of EL, always take EL off the percentile loss.

setup: A USD 1m credit book is cut into ten equal USD 100,000 positions, all of them claims on the same obligor. The obligor has a 1-year default probability of 5% and recovery is zero. Credit VaR is the 99th percentile loss minus the expected loss.
ask: The 99th percentile loss is closest to:

options.label: USD 100,000
options.why: Assumed one position defaults at a time, as if diversified. All ten sit on one obligor and default together.

options.label: USD 50,000
options.why: That is the expected loss (5% x 1m), not a percentile.

options.label: USD 0
options.why: No loss occurs 95% of the time, but a 99th percentile needs 99% coverage. The loss only takes the values 0 and 1m, so the percentile is 1m.

working.label: Loss distribution
working.display: Loss = 0 with probability 95%, USD 1m with probability 5%

takeaway: One obligor means one perfectly correlated bet: the loss is all or nothing, and a 5% default chance puts the whole exposure at the 99th percentile.

setup: A portfolio holds one 1-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 6.5m. Its 1-year default probability is 7% and recovery is 88%. Credit VaR (99%) is the 99th percentile loss minus the expected loss.
ask: The 99% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 7,300
options.why: Scale slip (1/100): a percent-versus-decimal mix-up.

options.label: ≈ USD 55,000
options.why: Reported the expected loss (7% x 780,000) instead of the percentile loss less EL.

options.label: ≈ USD 6,045,000
options.why: Forgot the 88% recovery, so the loss on default was the full 6.5m: 6.5m - 455,000.

takeaway: With a single bond whose PD exceeds the tail probability, the percentile loss is the full loss given default; credit VaR is that minus EL.

setup: A homogeneous loan book has EAD USD 350m, an expected default rate of 2.5% and recovery of 60%. The 99.9% worst-case default rate (WCDR) is 10.25%. Here credit VaR is defined as the loss not exceeded at 99.9%, namely WCDR x EAD x LGD.
ask: Compared with the unexpected loss (worst-case loss minus expected loss), this credit VaR is:

options.label: The same
options.why: Assumed credit VaR always nets off EL. Under this definition it is the whole worst-case loss, so EL stays inside it.

options.label: Smaller, by the expected loss
options.why: Reversed the comparison: the unexpected loss is the one with EL removed, so it is the smaller figure.

takeaway: Check which definition the question states: WCDR x EAD x LGD includes EL; the unexpected-loss version takes it off.

setup: Two loans. Loan 1: EAD USD 200m, LGD 45%, PD 2%, 99.9% WCDR 8%. Loan 2: EAD USD 100m, LGD 60%, PD 3%, 99.9% WCDR 12%. Credit VaR is the sum of the loans' worst-case losses, WCDR x EAD x LGD.
ask: The 1-year 99.9% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.4 million
options.why: Decimal slip: entered the WCDRs as 0.8% and 1.2%, ten times too small.

options.label: ≈ USD 3.6 million
options.why: Used the average PDs (2% and 3%) in place of the worst-case rates, which gives the expected loss.

options.label: ≈ USD 36 million
options.why: Applied the 12% WCDR to the whole USD 300m and skipped LGD.

takeaway: Worst-case loss per loan is WCDR x EAD x LGD. Swap in PD and you get the expected loss, far below the tail figure.

setup: Two borrowers, A and B, each have a 9.0% probability of default. Their default correlation is 0.28.
ask: The joint probability that both default is closest to:

options.why: Assumed independence: $0.09 \times 0.09$. The positive correlation was ignored.
Used the perfect-correlation limit, where B defaults whenever A does.
Read the correlation 0.28 as the joint probability.

takeaway: Joint PD = $\pi_1\pi_2 + \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$. At correlation 0.28 the covariance term is almost three times the independent one.

setup: Companies A and B have default probabilities of 5% and 10%. Their default correlation is 0.6, a high value.
ask: The joint probability of default lies:

options.label: Below 0.5%
options.why: Took 0.5% (the independent product 5% x 10%) as the ceiling. A positive correlation pushes the joint PD above it.

options.label: Above 5%
options.why: Added the PDs or let the correlation inflate it past A's own PD. Both must default, so it cannot exceed the smaller PD of 5%.

takeaway: Joint PD is bounded: at least the independent product (for positive correlation) and at most the smaller of the two PDs.

setup: Two credits have default probabilities of 0.4% and 1.0%, with default correlation 10%. You build the joint PD from two terms: the independent product $\pi_1\pi_2$ and the correlation term $\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$.
ask: Which term is larger?

options.label: The correlation term, by roughly 15 times
The independent product, because the PDs are small
options.why: Compared the PDs as small numbers. The standard deviations $\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}$ are about 6% and 10%, far larger than the PDs, so the correlation term wins.

options.label: They are about equal
options.why: Neither term is close: 0.0628% against 0.004%.

takeaway: For rare defaults the standard deviations are roughly the square roots of the PDs, so the correlation term dwarfs $\pi_1\pi_2$ even at modest correlation.

setup: Loans to X and Y have default probabilities of 10% and 4%. The probability that both default is 3.93%. Independence would give 0.4%, and the largest possible joint probability is 4%.
ask: The implied default correlation is:

options.label: Close to zero
options.why: Looked at the small joint probability in absolute terms. It must be compared with the 0.4% independence benchmark, and it is almost ten times that.

options.label: Moderate, around 0.3
options.why: Took the midpoint of the range. The joint PD is 3.93% against a ceiling of 4%, which sits at the very top of the range.

takeaway: Judge a joint PD against its two benchmarks: the independent product (rho = 0) and the smaller PD (rho near 1).

setup: A CCC credit and a BBB credit have default probabilities of 0.8% and 0.4% over the horizon. The probability that both default is 0.035%.
ask: The default correlation is closest to:

options.why: Stopped at the covariance ($0.00035 - 0.8\% \times 0.4\% = 0.000318$) and never divided by the standard deviations.
Decimal slip in the denominator: used 0.000562 instead of 0.00562 for $\sigma_1\sigma_2$.
Divided the covariance by $\pi_1\pi_2$ instead of by $\sigma_1\sigma_2$. A correlation above 100% cannot be right.

takeaway: Correlation = covariance / ($\sigma_1\sigma_2$), with $\sigma = \sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}$. It can never leave the range -1 to +1.

setup: Two credits have default probabilities of 0.3% and 0.4% and a joint default probability of 0.2%. Default correlation is covariance divided by $\sigma_1\sigma_2$, where $\sigma = \sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}$.
ask: The denominator $\sigma_1\sigma_2$ is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied the two variances $\pi(1-\pi)$ and skipped the square roots.
Added the two standard deviations (0.055 + 0.063) instead of multiplying them.

takeaway: The denominator is a product of standard deviations, each about the square root of a small PD, so it is a few thousandths here.

setup: 1,000 equal loans to borrowers all rated BB at the start of year 1. Cumulative default rates for BB: 0.63% after year 1, 1.93% after year 2, 3.46% after year 3. Ratings changes are ignored. You want the defaults that occur during year 3 only.
ask: The year-3-only default rate is closest to:

options.why: Used the cumulative three-year figure, which includes defaults from years 1 and 2.
Picked the year-2 cumulative figure instead of the year-3 increment.
Used the year-1 figure, which is the first-year default rate, not year 3.

takeaway: Cumulative default rates need differencing: the default rate in a single year is the increase in the cumulative curve.

setup: A firm has USD 2.0m of senior debt and USD 0.5m of subordinated debt. In liquidation its assets realise USD 2.25m, distributed strictly by seniority.
ask: The subordinated debt recovers:

options.label: Nothing
options.why: Assumed juniors are wiped out whenever assets fall short of total debt (2.5m). Assets still exceed the senior claim by 0.25m, which goes to the juniors.

options.label: All of its face value
options.why: Ignored that total debt (2.5m) exceeds the assets (2.25m), so someone takes a loss, and it is the junior class.

takeaway: Pay senior first, then see what is left: junior debt takes the shortfall, here a 50% recovery.

setup: Expected loss rate = PD x (1 - recovery). In normal times PD is 2% and recovery 40%. In a recession stress PD rises to 5%, and historically recovery rates fall when default rates rise, to 30% here. Holding recovery at 40% would give a loss rate of 3.0%.
ask: The stressed expected loss rate with 30% recovery is:

options.label: Equal to 3.0%
options.why: Kept recovery at its normal level. Defaults and recoveries move against each other, so the stress must lower recovery.

options.label: Lower than 3.0%
options.why: Read a lower recovery rate as a smaller loss. Lower recovery means a larger loss given default.

takeaway: Recovery is negatively correlated with default. In a stress, raise PD and cut recovery together.
